Item 1. Business

Sample Co designs and manufactures widgets and gadgets across the consumer and industrial markets. The company was incorporated in Delaware in 1986 and operates through three segments: Widgets, Gadgets, and Services. Each segment sells through a mix of direct, retail, and reseller channels, with widgets representing the largest share of revenue at roughly sixty percent. The company has approximately twelve thousand employees worldwide as of the end of fiscal year 2024, with primary engineering, manufacturing, and corporate offices in California, Texas, and Ireland. We invest a meaningful portion of revenue back into research and development, with an emphasis on materials science, embedded firmware, and supply-chain analytics. Our products are sold in more than forty countries and we maintain regional support centers in North America, Europe, and Asia. Competition in our markets is broad and includes both incumbent industrial suppliers and a growing set of new entrants applying machine-vision and connectivity techniques to traditional form factors. We compete primarily on quality, breadth of catalog, and service responsiveness, and we view our long-standing channel relationships as a durable advantage.

Item 1A. Risk Factors

Our business is subject to a number of risks. Macroeconomic conditions including inflation, interest rate volatility, and shifts in consumer demand can affect both unit demand and our cost structure. Supply chain disruption remains a meaningful risk: a substantial portion of our subassemblies are sourced from contract manufacturers concentrated in two countries, and a disruption to those facilities for any reason — natural disaster, geopolitical event, public-health event — could materially affect our ability to meet demand. We rely on third-party logistics providers for outbound shipping; service interruptions or rate changes there flow through to our gross margin on a lag. Information security is a continuing risk; we operate engineering and customer-facing systems that are persistent targets, and a successful intrusion could lead to loss of trade secrets, customer-data exposure, remediation costs, and regulatory action. Foreign-exchange exposure is material: roughly forty-five percent of revenue is denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar, and our hedging program reduces but does not eliminate translation impact. Litigation is a persistent risk, including intellectual-property suits in jurisdictions with active patent assertion markets.

Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations

Fiscal year 2024 revenue was $4.2 billion, an increase of 8% versus the prior year, driven primarily by stronger Widgets unit demand in North America and Europe. Gross margin expanded by 90 basis points year over year, reflecting both pricing actions taken in the second half of fiscal 2023 and a favorable shift in product mix toward higher-margin variants. Operating expenses grew 6%, with research and development up 11% as we continued to invest in next-generation product platforms, partially offset by lower marketing spend in the second half. We generated $720 million of cash flow from operations and returned $300 million to shareholders through a combination of share repurchases and dividends. We ended the year with $1.1 billion in cash and short-term investments and $400 million of long-term debt outstanding. Looking forward, we expect modest continued revenue growth, with margin steady-to-up, contingent on the input-cost environment and on the pace of investment in our new product platforms. We continue to monitor macroeconomic indicators closely and have contingency plans across procurement, staffing, and pricing in place if demand softens.

Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data

The consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes are included beginning on page F-1 of this Annual Report on Form 10-K and are incorporated herein by reference. The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States and have been audited by our independent registered public accounting firm. Significant accounting policies, including those relating to revenue recognition, inventory valuation, business combinations, intangible asset impairment, income taxes, and stock-based compensation, are described in Note 1 of the consolidated financial statements. Management has concluded that internal control over financial reporting was effective as of the end of the fiscal year. Critical audit matters identified by the auditor include inventory reserves and the valuation of acquired intangible assets, both of which require significant estimation and judgment.
